hook_text: Satellite pictures sometimes show farms and forests glowing red. Nothing is on fire. The satellite can see a light your eyes cannot.
clip_script: A satellite picture is not a photo the way your phone takes one. It is millions of tiny squares, pixels, and each square is a measurement of the light bouncing off one patch of ground. And satellites measure light your eyes cannot see. Healthy plants bounce back huge amounts of an invisible light called near-infrared. So scientists play a trick: they colour that invisible light red. Suddenly every healthy field, forest and garden glows bright red, and water turns almost black. That is a false-colour image. Farmers use it to spot the struggling patch of a maize field before the leaves even change colour. And the satellites never stop. One kind hangs thirty-six thousand kilometres above the equator and sends a fresh picture of Africa every fifteen minutes. That is your weather report. The next time you see the clouds swirling on TV, remember: that picture was taken from space a few minutes ago.
visual_style: A whiteboard satellite beaming down onto a grid of pixels over farmland; the fields flip from green to bright red in a false-colour reveal; a geostationary satellite fixed above a spinning globe.
pacing: Quick hook, a satisfying reveal of red vegetation, then the fifteen-minute weather camera.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to read the planet from space.
